division_reconstructed.note: No source places this household anywhere — the record gives a name and no address, no street and not even a division. So BOTH halves of this band are dealt rather than read: the south division from the reconstruction order book's own household target by division, and the class from the town model's employment distribution, which puts this household under the placement policy's tradesman_dwellings clause. The frame cottages fall on the side streets behind the principal frontages — the back of the same blocks the stores front, which is how a block parcel comes to deal its meanest roof to its worst street. The deal is seeded on this household's own id, so it is the same on every run — and it is the weakest seat this ladder makes: no lot, no roof, no coordinate and no source behind either half of it.

head: keyes_edward

arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. tax_1833 stands against this person's name by 31 December 1833 and nothing says when they came. THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. It bounds the town's RECORD of this name and not the day this person reached Chicago. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the town's own paper carries this name by 1 July 1835; whether the man it names was standing in the town is a claim this record cannot make, and present_on_scene_date says `uncertain` for that reason.

present_on_scene_date.note: THE RECORD DOES NOT REACH THE DAY. Every source that names this person falls on one side of 1 July 1835, and nothing follows them to it or says they left. `uncertain` rather than dropped — the distinction index.json draws for Jeremiah Porter, and a finding, not a gap. AND THE BRACKET THIS CARD ONCE HAD IS WITHDRAWN, NOT LOST: its at-or-before leg was tax_1833 alone. THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. It bounds the town's RECORD of this name and not the day this person reached Chicago, so it cannot say this person was here to be followed across the day. Withdrawn to `uncertain` and not to `absent` — no source places this person anywhere else on 1 July 1835 either, and a man who was taxed for ground in the town may perfectly well have been standing on it.

modelled_family.note: The kin core only. A servant, an apprentice or a journeyman this house may have held is priced by T-1183 and seated by T-1173; a boarder is seated by T-1175. The drawn size is a floor on the house.

married.what_happened: NOT DRAWN FOR THIS HOUSE: MOVED INTO IT. The household model drew this house married and the order book had no woman left in its wife's cell, so no wife was drawn. Mary Burke headed a house of her own, dealt by T-1174 to fill the women and children the age pyramid lacked; she fits this house by its own rules — her division, a band never above his, no child older than his band allows — and T-2020 folds her house into his: she is his wife here and the 3 of her house come with her. Every name, age band and seed is the one T-1174 drew; the children keep the surname they were dealt with. Both people are the town's invention at the `reconstructed` tier, and the marriage is too: no source says Edward Keyes married anybody.

dated_bounds.list_title: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833
dated_bounds.identity_discriminator: forenames agree initial for initial: entry 'Edward Keyes' against resident 'Edward Keyes'
dated_bounds.identity_rule: one resident of the surname 'Keyes' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered.
dated_bounds.note: PROPERTY, NOT PRESENCE (T-1117). Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 names the owners of ground inside the town, resident or not — its entry 110 is Alexander Wolcott, who had been dead since 25 October 1830 — so this row bounds what this person was assessed for and says nothing about where the person was. tools/assert_tax_roll_ruling.py holds that ruling on the two readings it rests on. THE IDENTITY IS INFERRED AND THE PAGE IS NOT. The reading of the roll is documented — the town's own paper, held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository, twice mediated by Schulz's transcription and Genealogy Trails' republication, which this project has not gone behind. What no source states is that the man on the roll is the person on this card: data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json joins them on a name, by its rule “one resident of the surname 'Keyes' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered.”, and forenames agree initial for initial: entry 'Edward Keyes' against resident 'Edward Keyes'. A bound whose subject is inferred is an inferred bound. No grade moves here and the identity is neither reopened nor hardened.

persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented once and corroborated by nothing else, so the weakest rung of `inferred` the owner's ladder defines. A SINGLE APPEARANCE AND NOTHING ELSE. Read from tax_1833. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G3), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. tax_1833 stands against this person's name by 31 December 1833 and nothing says when they came. THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. It bounds the town's RECORD of this name and not the day this person reached Chicago. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the town's own paper carries this name by 1 July 1835; whether the man it names was standing in the town is a claim this record cannot make, and present_on_scene_date says `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Keyes, Edward” (tax_1833_056, line 108). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Keyes' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('keyes_edward:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a poll, tax or muster list names a person 20 or over - the 1840 schedule's own adult line. THE FRANCHISE'S AGE RULE IS NOT IN ANY SOURCE RECORD THIS PROJECT HOLDS; this is the model's conditioning and not a reading (T-1303's finding, handed to T-1304). No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

sex_basis.note: A FORENAME THAT STANDS IN ONE SEX'S NAMING ONLY. Nothing about this person is recorded; the name is the whole of the reasoning, and the table that licenses it — data/research/residents/forename_sex.json — refuses a name its own evidence splits, refuses Jean, Marion, Leslie and Francis by name, and refuses an initial outright.
